title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Deployment Guide, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrades, Rollback, and Customer Requirements
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended patterns and concrete runbooks for private deployments (VPC-hosted and on‑prem). It covers reference architectures, packaging guidance for on‑prem appliances, day‑2 operational procedures, and prescriptive upgrade and rollback playbooks. It also contains a reusable customer requirements checklist used by Solutions and SRE to scope engagements.

Intended audience: platform engineers, solutions architects, SRE, customer ops, and account teams supporting dedicated/private deployments.

Scope:
- VPC-hosted private control plane + customer-managed compute (common for cloud customers)
- Air-gapped / on‑prem appliance packaging and install paths
- Day‑2 operations: monitoring, capacity scaling, backups, and incident response
- Upgrade and rollback procedures with validation steps and automated gates
- Customer requirements library (network, security, compliance, capacity)

--

1) Reference Architectures (Summary)

A. VPC-hosted Customer (recommended for most enterprise customers)
- Components: customer VPC, NAT & egress gateways, private peering to Redwood control plane, dedicated GPU subnet(s), private load balancer, bastion hosts for support access (jump box).
- Typical sizing: 4–64 GPU nodes depending on throughput. See capacity table below for baseline ratios.
- High‑availability: spread worker nodes across at least 2 AZs; control plane endpoints should be pinned to customer-specific endpoints with fallback.

B. On‑Prem Appliance (air‑gapped)
- Components: appliance (1–N racks), on‑prem orchestration (k8s or NUC-based single-node for small PoC), local NFS/object storage for model artifacts, HSM/KMS integration optional.
- Packaging: containerized runtime with precompiled kernel bundles per supported GPU type (A100, H100, L4).
- Isolation: FIPS-ready binaries and offline activation keys for air‑gapped installs.

Reference architecture diagram (textual):
- Control plane (Redwood-managed) <-> Private peering/VPN <-> Customer VPC NAT/Egress -> GPU worker subnets -> Load balancer -> GPUs
- On‑prem: Control plane running locally (optional) -> Local model store -> Worker pool -> GPU fabric

--

2) VPC Deployment Guide (Cloud customer)

Pre-requisites:
- Customer provides VPC, subnets (control, worker, management), IAM role(s) for provisioning, and a NAT egress path for Redwood agent.
- Required firewall rules: outbound TLS (443) to control plane endpoints (list provided on request), inbound from bastion only for support ports (SSH 22 restricted to IP allowlist).

Step-by-step (minimal):
1. Provision VPC subnets: management (/24), control (/27), worker (/20).
2. Create service role and grant necessary permissions (EC2, EBS, ENI, KMS if using CMK).
3. Install Redwood agent (helm chart or systemd package) into management subnet.
4. Register worker nodes with control plane using signed claim tokens; verify KV cache and model pull.
5. Configure autoscaling policies: target CPU 60% and GPU utilization 70% with headroom burst +5 nodes.
6. Run end-to-end test: warm model cache with benchmark prompt sets, validate latency SLOs (p95 < 120ms for short prompts typical).

Example IAM snippet (JSON):
```json
{
  "Statement": [
    {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["ec2:CreateNetworkInterface", "ec2:AttachVolume"], "Resource": "*"}
  ]
}
```

Network table:
| Role | CIDR | Purpose | Notes |
|------|------|---------|-------|
| management subnet | 10.10.1.0/24 | agent & control plane egress | restrict inbound SSH to support CIDRs |
| control subnet | 10.10.2.0/27 | internal control traffic | AZ-spread recommended |
| worker subnet | 10.10.16.0/20 | GPU instances | tagged for billing & autoscaling |

--

3) On‑Prem Packaging & Install Patterns

Supported package types:
- OCI images with signed manifests for customers with local registries
- Offline tarball releases with checksums and GPG signatures for air‑gapped installs
- Appliance bits for validated hardware SKUs (reference racks: model H100-4U, A100-2U)

Recommended install modes:
- k8s (production): helm chart + node-feature-discovery + device plugin for GPUs
- Single-node appliance (PoC): systemd-managed container runtime with supervisor scripts

Key steps for air‑gapped install:
1. Ship release bundle (tar.gz) with manifests and license key.
2. Customer loads bundle onto local registry or host.
3. Run installer with --offline flag; installer validates signatures and performs local KMS handshake if configured.
4. Start model sync job to pull verified artifacts from the customer-provided model bundle.

Packaging note: include quantized model variants and kernel blobs matching the target GPU family to avoid runtime kernel fetches.

--

4) Day‑2 Operations (Runbook highlights)

Monitoring & Alerts (SRE recommended):
- Metrics to monitor: GPU utilization (per-device), host OOM events, inference p95 latency, KV cache hit ratio, model pull failures, disk IOPS on model store.
- Alert thresholds (example):
  - GPU memory pressure > 85% for 5m -> Sev2
  - p95 latency > 2x baseline for 3m -> Sev2
  - KV cache miss rate > 30% -> Sev3

Backups and model artifacts:
- Model artifacts are immutable; maintain an object store snapshot cadence (daily diff + weekly full).
- Catalog database (metadata) backup: snapshot every 6 hours; retention 30 days.

Routine day‑2 tasks:
1. Patch and security updates: apply OS and runtime library patches in maintenance windows.
2. Scale worker pools based on scheduled traffic: prepare capacity before large rollouts.
3. Validate cold start: periodically run a cold-cache runbook to ensure model cold start < defined SLA.

Operational checklist (weekly):
- Check disk usage < 70% on model store nodes
- Validate agent version parity across nodes
- Inspect SLO dashboards & document any regressions

--

5) Upgrade Procedure (Blue/Green-ish with automated gates)

Principles:
- Non-destructive by default: preserve model artifacts and config during upgrades.
- Canary first: 1–5% traffic to new release for 30–60m with synthetic and real traffic checks.
- Automated rollback on key metric regressions.

Pre-upgrade checklist:
- Backup metadata and model store snapshot
- Capture baseline metrics (p50/p95 latency, error rate, GPU utilization) for the past 72h
- Ensure at least 2 restore points for container images and config

Upgrade steps (high level):
1. Create new deployment (new node pool or new k8s namespace) with target runtime version.
2. Run smoke tests (bootstrap prompts, model load, simple evals).
3. Enable canary routing (1–5% traffic). Monitor for 60 minutes.
4. If canary passes, ramp to 25% for 30 minutes, then 50% for 30 minutes, then full cutover.
5. Post-upgrade validation: run regression eval suite (predefined prompt sets) and compare quality metrics.

Automated gates (examples):
- Reject if p95 latency increases > 20% over baseline OR error rate increases > 0.5% absolute.
- Reject if KV cache miss rate increases > 15% absolute.

Rollback procedure (immediate):
1. Disable new node pool from routing.
2. Reattach traffic to previous stable pool.
3. If nodes cannot be reattached, re-deploy previous container image to new pool and re-run smoke tests.
4. Post-mortem: collect debug logs, traces, and evaluation diffs into a ticket.

--

6) Rollback Playbook (detailed steps)

When to trigger: severe latency regressions (p95 > threshold), increased error rates > SLA, model correctness regression flagged by quality monitoring.

Immediate actions (0–15m):
1. Escalation: notify oncall and product owner.
2. Traffic cut: route traffic away from new nodes (use load balancer weights).
3. Verify stable pool health and start traffic rollback.
4. Start automated rollback job and capture state (git tag, image digest).

Recovery (15–90m):
1. Confirm user-facing metrics return to baseline.
2. Collect traces from affected requests and mark suspicious prompts for triage.
3. Disable any feature flags introduced with the release.

Post-rollback (24–72h):
- Run a full regression analysis and open a blameless postmortem if needed.

--

7) Customer Requirements Library (scoping checklist)

Use this checklist during scoping calls. Answer required fields and attach to the customer ticket.

| Requirement | Example / Expected Value | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------|
| Primary deployment mode | VPC-hosted / On‑prem appliance | Choose one |
| Expected throughput | e.g., 100 qps sustained, 1k peak | Used for sizing GPU pool |
| Latency SLOs | p95 < 150ms for <512 tokens | Drive autoscale policies |
| Data residency | EU only / US | May require private control plane |
| Network constraints | No outbound internet, egress via proxy | Affects packaging (offline) |
| KMS/HSM | AWS KMS / Vault HSM | Provide access patterns & key rotation cadence |
| Compliance requirements | SOC2 / PCI / HIPAA | May require additional evidence & runbooks |
| Backup retention | 30d metadata / 90d artifact | Affects storage costs |
| Hardware constraints | GPU SKU allowed (A100/H100), rack units | Impact packaging & kernel distributions |

--

8) Ownership, SLAs & Contacts

- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team (pager: eng-private-deployments@redwood.ai)
- SRE oncall: see team rota (internal link)
- Solutions engineering: assigned per account; include contact in customer tickets

SLO examples for private deployments:
- Control plane availability: 99.95% monthly (for Redwood-managed control plane)
- Worker stable health: 99.9% monthly (customer-managed hardware)
- Latency SLOs: agreed per-customer in SLAs

--

9) Troubleshooting Quick Reference

Symptoms -> Quick checks:
- Model load failures: check model store disk, permission (uid/gid) on files, and model manifest checksum.
- High cold-start latency: verify kernel blobs installed for GPU family, warm model cache, prefetch config.
- Intermittent agent disconnects: check NAT session timeouts and MTU on customer firewall.

Commands & snippets:
- Agent status: `redwood-agent status --format json`
- Force model sync: `redwoodctl models sync --model-id <id> --force`

--

Appendix: Example capacity baseline (guideline only):
- Small (PoC): 1–2 GPU nodes (A10 / L4) for 20–50 qps
- Medium: 4–8 A100 nodes for 200–800 qps
- Large: 16+ H100 nodes for 1k+ qps with batching
